“Will there be something I actually want to drink?”

“Can I trust the answer about what’s in this food?”

Different questions. Different needs. Both belong in the conversation about hospitality.

This week on Eating at a Meeting Podcast LIVE, Katy Jones joins me for a conversation that starts with sobriety and events—and leads into food allergies, transparency, and trust.

Katy has spoken about the frustration of limited beverage choices as a sober guest. She has also described how clear food information helped her son, who has a tree nut allergy, feel confident enough to try new foods during a family trip.

Those experiences give us a starting point for asking:

▶ What makes a guest feel genuinely considered?
▶ How do we offer choices without demanding personal explanations?
▶ How does accurate ingredient information reach the person who needs it?
▶ Where can technology help—and where must people follow through?

We’ll connect those questions to Katy’s work as CEO of Trustwell, without losing sight of the person at the table.

Planners, this is language for your next BEO and site visit. Suppliers, this is what guests notice before they decide whether to come back.

Come watch LIVE and bring your questions. What’s one thing you’d ask a venue about food or drinks before your next event?

🎙️ From Sober Choices to Food Allergies: Building Trust with Event F&B

elements.content:
A strong restaurant coffee program starts before the first cup is brewed.

The best fit is not always the darkest roast or the most complex blend. It is the coffee that matches the dining experience, the equipment on site, the speed of service, and the way guests typically order.

For a busy brunch operation, consistency and brew time may matter more than variety. For a fine dining room, coffee often needs to complement dessert without overpowering it. For a hotel lobby, the priority may be a dependable profile that tastes familiar across many cups.

One useful exercise: taste coffee the way your guest experiences it. Try it after a full meal, with milk, alongside dessert, and after it has sat briefly in a server station.

Coffee is often the final impression of a meal. That makes fit just as important as flavor.

What does your team consider first when choosing coffee for a foodservice setting?

elements.content:
A café is not a small restaurant, and its till shouldn't be either.

A typical independent restaurant might do 80 covers at £30. A café does around 300 transactions at about £6, with 120 of them between 8am and 9:20. In that window, taps per transaction is the only metric that matters.

The number that stood out in our new guide: missing a 40p oat milk charge on 60 drinks a day costs around £8,000 a year. It happens when modifiers are buried screens deep and baristas fall back on free-text notes.

What to demand instead:
→ Every modifier one tap deep and individually priced
→ Eat-in/takeaway as one toggle that fixes price and VAT
→ Loyalty and customer data you own, plus order-ahead slots
→ Card fees quoted on your real £6 ticket

And one test for any demo: time a flat white with oat milk and count the taps.

elements.content:
A customer sees a £3 cup of coffee, but a café owner sees everything it takes to serve it. ☕
It's easy to look at the price of a coffee and assume there's a healthy profit in every cup, especially when the beans and milk cost considerably less than what the customer pays.
But anyone running a café knows that the ingredients are only part of the picture.
You've got baristas to pay, rent and electricity to cover, cups and lids to buy, equipment to maintain, supplier deliveries to manage and card processing fees on every transaction.
The image illustrates how those costs can be spread across a £3 coffee. The percentages are examples rather than industry averages, but the point is worth considering.
When you're selling something at a relatively low price, even small increases in costs can make a noticeable difference to your margins.
That's why it's worth looking beyond how many coffees you're selling and thinking about how often your customers come back.

At Fill My Restaurant, we help hospitality businesses stay connected with their customers and encourage repeat visits, because a loyal customer who stops by regularly can be far more valuable than someone who visits once and never returns.

This week I read dozens of 1-star reviews for restaurants around Fort Myers and Cape Coral.
Here’s what surprised me: most of them weren’t about the food.
They said things like:
🍽️ “Appetizers came out before our drinks.”

🍽️ “We asked for a manager and no one came.”

✔️ Tickets that aren’t timed together
✔️ No bag check before the window
✔️ No portion standard on the line
✔️ No plan for when something goes wrong
The good news: systems problems are the most fixable problems a restaurant has. You don’t need a new chef or a new menu. You need a clear standard and a setup that makes the right way the easy way.
I spent 8 years in restaurants, from team member to General Manager, and that’s the work I love most: finding the gap between great food and a great experience, and closing it.

elements.content:
Most restaurants don’t have a hiring problem. They have a first-week problem. 🔑

We spend time and money recruiting, then hand the new hire an apron, a quick tour, and a “just follow Sam today.”

Then we’re surprised when they leave within the first month.

The first 7 days decide whether someone becomes a committed team member or a statistic. Here’s the simple structure I recommend:

📌 Day 1: Welcome, not survival. Introduce the team, show where everything is, and explain why their role matters. Nobody should spend the first day feeling lost.

📌 Days 2-3: Learn the standards. Show what “good” looks like for the menu, the service steps, and the guest experience. Don’t assume they’ll figure it out.

📌 Days 4-5: Practice with support. Pair them with a strong buddy, not just whoever is available. Let them do real tasks with feedback in the moment.

📌 Days 6-7: Check in. A short, honest conversation: What’s clear? What’s confusing? What do you need from us?

Why does this matter?
✅ Clear expectations reduce stress and early mistakes.
✅ People who feel supported stay longer.
✅ A confident new hire gives better service from the start.
✅ The cost of replacing one employee is far higher than the cost of a good first week.

Great teams aren’t built by finding perfect people. They’re built by giving good people a great start.

Fast for most, or fair for all? 👇

elements.content:
🍽️ IS THE HOSPITALITY INDUSTRY READY FOR THE GLP-1 GENERATION?

We talk constantly about rising food costs, labour shortages, changing consumer expectations and declining alcohol consumption.

But there’s another shift happening that I believe the hospitality industry needs to start paying attention to.

The growing use of GLP-1 weight-loss medications.

Medications such as Mounjaro and Wegovy are changing how some consumers approach food, portion sizes, appetite and potentially alcohol consumption.

And that raises an interesting question.

What happens to hospitality when customers still want the experience, but no longer want the quantity?

For decades, much of our industry has focused on generous portions, upselling additional courses, premium drinks packages and encouraging customers to spend more.

But consumer behaviour may be evolving.

Could we see:

🍽️ Smaller, beautifully presented portions without compromising quality?

🥗 More protein-focused, nutritionally balanced menu choices?

🍸 Greater demand for sophisticated alcohol-free beverages?

🏨 Hotels reconsidering traditional dining packages and buffet offerings?

💷 New approaches to menu engineering, pricing and profitability?

The challenge isn’t simply about serving less food.

It’s about understanding how changing consumer behaviour could influence the entire hospitality experience.

And importantly, smaller appetites don’t necessarily mean smaller expectations.

Customers may still want exceptional service, beautiful surroundings, memorable experiences and outstanding food.

They may simply consume differently.

For operators, this presents both a potential challenge and an opportunity.

The businesses that recognise emerging consumer trends and adapt intelligently could find themselves ahead of the curve.

Of course, GLP-1 users are not one homogeneous customer group, and more research is needed to understand the long-term impact on hospitality spending.

But I believe this is a conversation worth having now.

So, hospitality colleagues, here’s my question:

Are we beginning to see a genuine shift in dining behaviour, and should operators already be reconsidering their menus, portion sizes and beverage strategies?
